SUGGESTED MEASURES TO MINIMIZE PRICE INCREASES TO CANADIANS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the unilateral and untimely decision by the government to remove the subsidy to the milling industry, which will cause not only instability within the processing industry but also dramatic price increases to Canadian consumers, especially those who can least afford these increases at this time, I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath):

subsubtopic: MANUFACTURING SALES TAX REDUCTION-EFFECT ON ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Revenue who is also Minister of State for Small Business: it involves both his portfolios. My question refers to the manufacturing sales tax and the fact that it now appears the implementation of this sales tax will have serious consequences for the general economy of Canada.
Would the minister indicate whether any consideration has been given to rebating the sales tax which has already been paid in the case of inventories held by various retailers and wholesalers in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. A. C. Abbott (Minister of National Revenue and Minister of State (Small Business)):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: MANUFACTURING SALES TAX REDUCTION-EFFECT ON ECONOMY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member is aware of the difficult task this presents, because it is impossible in many cases to disgorge the tax which might have been paid at the manufacturing level on inventories in stock. 1 recognize that it has sometimes imposed on retailers a feeling of moral obligation to pass on the discount immediately because of the reduction of the tax. However, I think most reasonable purchasers understand that if the tax has already been paid on the inventory, the price cannot be reduced to take advantage of a tax reduction at the manufacturing level.

subsubtopic: MANUFACTURING SALES TAX REDUCTION-EFFECT ON ECONOMY
speechtext:
When the minister says it is a difficult matter to deal with, surely he is aware of the fact that section 17 of the Financial Administration Act covers the point: it allows for the remission of taxation. Surely he is aware of the fact that the previous minister of finance, in the 1974 and earlier budgets, set remissions with respect to reductions of sales tax at that time.
In view of the fact that a hiatus is developing and people are delaying their purchases until January or February, in the earnest hope they will get the benefit of this manufacturing sales tax reduction, will the minister not instruct his officials to get on with it and work out a proper remission plan under section 17 of the Financial Administration Act?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: MANUFACTURING SALES TAX REDUCTION-EFFECT ON ECONOMY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps the hon. member will allow me a little time to consult my officials on the point he raised and on the advice he has given. I will do so and perhaps be more fulsome in my answer at a later date.

Does he acknowledge that a hiatus is developing in the current period, in that the provincial sales tax had the effect of

I do not care what you call this committee, consultative committee or any other committee-a rose by any other name-and the same applies to a thorn. This is obviously not an in-house study. It is a fundamental study undertaken by admittedly distinguished Canadians on fundamental problems affecting the communications industry in Canada.
This morning I asked officials in her office if she had a press release, and someone from the PC research office went to her office at about eleven o'clock and was given a press release of her speech made two days previously. After twelve o'clock, my secretary, following another phone call, finally received the

minister's press release dated November 30, which gives in more detail the subject of the wire story which was brought to my attention this morning.
The press release refers to distinguished Canadians across the country, which was exactly the subject matter of my question. It sets out the qualifications of those distinguished Canadians. These are distinguished Canadians from coast to coast, from British Columbia to Nova Scotia and many great places in between. I do not question the character and intelligence of the people named to this consultative committee, which was given terms of reference to study the issue, and I believe they might produce a very interesting report. After all, there was the Fowler report in 1957, and 20 years before that there was the Massey report. That is why I and my party suggested more than two years ago that this whole tangled web of communications deserves another over-all objective look from someone outside of the interested parties and of the Department of Communications.
I should like to say, in conclusion, that the press release refers to distinguished Canadians and to a strategy to restructure the telecommunications system. It states the areas of study which involve new technologies, such as fibre optics, satellites, interactive television, and computer technology.
Some of the questions asked on the floor of the House today may very well have been within the terms of reference of this study, but I do not have the terms of reference in my hand; all I have is the press release.
The horrifying thing is: how can there be a study on communications with no formal hearings? The minister confirmed today that there is no intention of conducting public hearings. I agree with her that this matter has been studied ad infinitum, that there have been many substantive studies.
The fact that there have been studies on a topic does not preclude it from being aired and generated before distinguished Canadians, so that they can make up their own minds with the interplay of examination and cross-examination on many of these studies, some of which have been done by vested interests who have their own points of view to project.
Communications should be the most open field, yet a two-month study will be conducted behind closed doors. In coming to the conclusion of my question of privilege, I should like to indicate that either the minister knew her officials were asking distinguished Canadians to serve on a commission or a committee, or she did not.
I do not have to educate Mr. Speaker regarding the definitions of the word "commission", since they are used very freely, and the minister understands what 1 mean. Among other things, the Oxford Dictionary, taken from the table, defines "commission" in terms of royal as follows:
Commission of inquiry or committee appointed by the Crown at the instance of the government.
These eight distinguished Canadians did not come from the sky. They were not the creation of someone's imagination.
November 30, 1978

They were appointed by this minister of the Crown in the name of the government, and 1 presume they are being paid by the government.
I do not know whether the minister wants to play tricks with semantics. I gave her notice of my question of privilege so that she could stand in her place and indicate that she made a mistake on November 14. Either she knew that was going on almost two weeks ago and thus misled me, which affects how I discharge my duties as a member, or if she did not know something so fundamental was going on within her department, there is no use in a member on either side putting any questions to the hon. minister in this field. Perhaps she can admit her status today, that she did not know what was going on within her department, or that she misled me on November 14.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: MR. NOWLAN-ANSWER GIVEN BY MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize if the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan) did not receive the relevant press communique. It is a habit within my department that these are circulated, in the first place, to the hon. member who is the critic on communications on the other side of the House. I apologize profusely if he did not receive the communique. Indeed I am very surprised if he has not received it. As for my speeches, I suppose he is on my mailing list, but it takes a little more time for copies to be distributed to the different offices. However, I am grateful the hon. member goes to the trouble of reading my speeches.
I should like to comment very briefly on this matter. I fail to see that there is a question of privilege in the hon. member's intervention, since it is quite obvious that I did not mislead the House. On November 14 the hon. member asked me if I was aware that some of my officials were travelling across the country in order to invite prominent people to participate in a royal commission. My answer was, no, they were not inviting people to participate in a royal commission. I stand by that answer because, of course, there is no question of a royal commission in this particular case.
Today I announced the creation of an independent group of distinguished Canadians whom I have asked to produce specific recommendations on the strategy to restructure the Canadian telecommunications system and to contribute more effectively to the safeguarding of Canada's sovereignty. As I said during oral questions, this is a very small committee which was set up more in the nature of a task force in order to assist me in what is a very important and urgent task.
I do not want to imply that the hon. member does not know what a royal commission is, but he must be aware that a royal commission is established under the Great Seal of Canada and is constituted under the Inquiries Act. This committee has not been constituted in that fashion. As Minister of Communications I made nominations and asked seven or eight people to come and work with me on the objectives which I have just stated.
I repeat that there will be no public hearings and the committee will not be receiving evidence in the usual way. It is
Privilege-Mr. Nowlan
not a royal commission at all. These people will help me to consolidate several studies which have been conducted within my department and in other instances as well.
The studies on the recent and not so recent evolution of technology in the field of telecommunications are numerous. Somebody must sit down, read them over, and attempt to make a new synthesis of all innovations which will take place in the near or not so near future.
We are on the threshold of complete and great changes in this area. We are on the threshold of an information society. New services will come in at one time or another, but we do not know how soon. They all have to fit into what is already a very good system of telecommunications. A new architecture obviously will emerge from the gradual introduction of all of these new technologies and the new services which accompany them. That is why I asked these people to work in very close contact with the department and to use the studies which I commissioned within the department, so that I will be assisted in a task which has become more urgent because of the new proposed services a lot of people in the country are interested in introducing.
I must devise policies so that these new services will be introduced in a gradual fashion and in a manner which will not confuse or disrupt the entire system. The hon. member mentioned pay television, which is only one of the new services that will be available. Therefore it is my responsibility to foresee the appearance of these new services, and to perceive the changes which will take place in the entire structure of telecommunications. I need to accelerate my consolidation of all of these new innovations, so that I will be in a better position to implement these policies.
I feel there is no question of privilege. The only thing which is correct is what the hon. member has read from this communique, that the people who have accepted to participate in this committee, and to whom 1 am very grateful, indeed are very prominent and very well posted on the questions I will put to them. I suggest I should have a question of privilege rather than the hon. member, because he is attempting to lead the House into believing that I have indeed set up a royal commission.

On clause 2-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHILD TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is a rather surprising proposal at this particular time in that the government is faced with a general program of expenditure cuts. The government has proposed on the one hand that it would contribute to this cut by cutting back to the amount of $20 per child in the family allowance program, and on the other hand, to balance what it saw as a serious reduction in income for families in the low income bracket, it has proposed a tax credit of $200. This is payable even though there will not be any tax payable by the parent in the particular case.
Has the minister considered what the effect will be in four or five years of indexing both the $20 payment, plus the $18,000 income ceiling, plus the $200 tax credit? How does this fit in with the government's concept of establishing a control on expenditures? This control is not just on spending money-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: Order, please. I wonder if the hon. member is aware that we are on clause 2? The first marginal note is "Annual adjustment", which is the legal way of saying annual indexing of the $200 payment and of the $18,000 ceiling on income.
With the greatest respect, Mr. Chairman, I do not know how I could be more in order than I am. I am strictly talking about indexing and its effect. I think it is a legitimate question. The minister may be able to tell us what she told the Minister

of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board will be the effect of indexing the $200 a month and indexing the $18,000. That is within the program of real control of expenditures as recommended by the Auditor General last year and this year, of which we are very conscious at the present time.

Thus there may be more payments to be made at all levels. It is for that reason that I wonder if the parliamentary secretary can tell us that by 1980 the government estimates the additional cost will be some $35 million as against the cost forecast for next year, and that in 1981 the estimates are-of course they are gambling on what the cost of living index is going to be. The hon. member is correct that we did not table figures beyond 1979-80. I was just indicating that it works both ways. Sources of funds used to provide the tax credit are being indexed, but starting at a lower base, or the outlay is starting at a lower base. The source of the funds is being indexed as well. We get it both ways. The index affects both outlays and savings made from a reduction in the level of payments.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHILD TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I must confess to some mystification, unless I have the wrong end of the stick with regard to the program. First of all the minister proposes to reduce the family allowance to $20 from the present scale. Then there is the introduction of an index to the $18,000 ceiling, because anything over and above $18,000 will disqualify a family from receiving this $200 tax credit, or in any event there will be a declining entitlement because of it. Those two applications of an index represent an increased outlay, assuming that the index is going up.
There is a third component. Providing also that the index is going up, there will be an increasing outlay on the $200. First of all, by reason of the fact that the $200 is going to be indexed, it is in effect a payment to those families who do not pay any income tax and it is a diminution of revenues for those families who do pay income tax. It is, therefore, the equivalent of an outlay of moneys. On three counts, therefore, there is an outlay, or the equivalent of an outlay, of moneys, all three being indexed. This is my understanding of the program. That is what I think we in the opposition are entitled to have presented to us-the minister's forecast of the future cost of this program that she may or should have presented to her colleagues in order to get cabinet approval for it. No one can make me believe that cabinet accepted this plan merely on the projection of the 1979-80 figures which have been given as a statement. There is a table of either the next five years or ten years showing the effect on the cost of the family allowance program as a result of the changes. Surely if that has been used as a basis for presenting and having this program accepted by the cabinet, the minister should be in a position to table it, in order to convince her colleagues and the public that this is something worthwhile.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHILD TAX CREDIT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think this assurance has been given before during the debate. The whole concept of Bill C-10 was accepted on the basis, and indeed it is before parliament, that it will be basically self-financing over the years, not just for the immediate years ahead but for years to come. Perhaps the point that is possibly being missed by the hon. member for Edmonton West is the fact that the indexing of family allowance payments has been on the books for some time. Where substantial savings occur, which is something I do not believe is entirely clear to the hon. member, instead of the indexing starting in 1980 say on a base of what would otherwise have been $28, it will be applied on a base of $20. Thus the savings, for instance in the next year, could be $8.48 if we assume an inflation rate of 6 per cent next year. This figure would be $8.48 in 1980 rather than $8 this year. In effect the indexing is providing for a higher pay out of the $200 tax credit, but it is also providing for higher savings in government expenditures month by month in terms of what the family allowance payments would have otherwise been.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHILD TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not mind, comparing two things in actuality. What I am looking at is the abandonment of a family allowance plan as it exists
November 30, 1978

today. It is being set aside. The minister has declared, "All right, fine, by setting that aside we are going to save as of next year whatever it would have cost to index the family allowance program".
That is all that would have been saved next year as compared to this year if there had been a continuation. Now there is a new plan. I say in order to convince the House that this new plan is valid we should start from square one, which is 1979-80, the effective date of the new plan, and progress on a period of say five to ten years, and see how much that will cost. I am sure that the then minister of national health and welfare, when the program of indexing the family allowance first started some years ago, had to lay a schedule showing estimated costs over the years to his or her cabinet colleagues. Goodness, that is fundamental. I am trying to find out what costs this minister foresees for the next five to ten years for this family allowance program. She has given us the costs for 1979-80 but there are some shell-game operations going on with regard to expenditures in the past, and this year. This is a comparison in effect of apples and oranges. What I want to know is the cost of the oranges. This information has not been given to us, with the greatest of respect, with the exception of the first year, and in that case I have to sort out the figures. It is not as clear as has been indicated.
If the minister says, "We have estimated it, on the basis of our proposal of indexing, that the first year is going to result in an increase of expenditures under the family allowance program as it will start out effective with the new program of $25 million or $35 million," all right, we will accept those figures. Then we will say what about the second year, and let us go on down the line?
I do not think that my colleagues and I are prepared to buy a new program just on this basis without some idea of the cost. We do not know that some of these indices tied into particular items may not result in some sort of a shooting star on expenditures. On the other hand, with the expertise that is available to the minister, surely these tables have been produced. I am sure the President of the Treasury Board did not buy this change in the program on the basis of the minister saying, "I think it will cost $35 million the first year." What if someone said, "What about the following year?" What if she replied, "I don't know"? Her colleagues would be out of their minds to accept that kind of a statement notwithstanding all of the charm she might want to use on them. The minister has a reputation of being pretty hard-nosed about things like this. 1 am sure if the minister's colleagues approached her in cabinet session with a new program, her first question would be, "How much will this cost us in the foreseeable future?"
This is the information we are seeking. This is the information we would like the government to share with us. If it is not available, then I must say somebody has to go back to the drawing board.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I can only repeat that when the Minister of Finance entered the debate on November 9 he indicated very clearly that there would be no substantial difference in total because the family allowance program
Family Allowances
estimates were calculated through the use of models that bring into account all sorts of things, for instance, potential growth of income, rates of inflation, number of children, distribution of incomes, and all the other factors. After all, we are dealing with a bill to amend the Income Tax Act, and in particular with clause 2 of that bill. It is important to the Minister of Finance that there be no additional substantial costs as a result of changing this program around.
I defer to your judgment, Mr. Chairman, but I do not think we should be discussing the total cost of family allowance programs per se at this time. I think we are dealing with a technical amendment in Bill C-10, clause 2. We have endeavoured to point matters out as best we can to satisfy the hon. member for Edmonton West. Over and over again the statement has been made that not only in 1979-80 will there be very little change in the next effect of the program, but that indeed will continue in the years ahead. All the reasons for that have been put on the record more than once. I am not sure what else we can add on that score. If the hon. member would like to come up with a guesstimate as to what the rate of inflation might be for the next year or two, then the figures could be reworked, based on that. However, it would work out to roughly the same thing.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, could I be given a few minutes by the hon. member?

speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

I would just like to repeat once more what I understand of the question put by the hon. member regarding indexation. What seems to me to be important is the key concept that this program is self-financing. Second, out of the three sources from which we created the new child tax credit, two were indexed. That will continue in years to come. Each year where it is cancelled results in more savings.
The new program has two features which are also indexed. The child tax credit is indexed. It will be $218 next year per child. The ceiling of net income, which is our point of reference by which we start cutting off the credit, is indexed. The sources which make up the amount are composed of the $50 tax exemption, which is cancelled. That is a saving in itself. It is not the indexing of it. It will create savings through the years, not just one year. Then the special tax privilege for 16-year olds and 17-year olds which was indexed is cancelled and brought back to the level of other children. That amounts to a saving of close to $400 per child per year, plus indexing through the years. The third source of it is the family allowance reduction and the reduction of the base allows for not only a net saving in the allowances for this year but a major saving in its indexing in the coming years.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHILD TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
I thank the minister for reviewing elements of the program on both sides of the ledger. On the other hand, the mere statements which have been given

November 30, 1978
Family Allowances
to us are not sufficient. The minister says she is eliminating the indexing of family allowances at the present level. Very well. Let us assume that the present level continues for five years. A certain figure would be reached, and there is a projected cost; the cost can be forecast within certain limits of accuracy. Then, based upon population figures, estimates can be made of the number of children who would qualify under the program. The effect of the elimination of the $50 allowance would also be determinable, and the special indexation plan for the 16 and 17-year olds is similarly predictable. Let us see this in tabular form. Then, on the basis of an annual increase in the cost of living of 8 per cent, family allowances will cost us so much starting at $20. A ceiling of $18,000 for low income families will amount to so much. Tax credit will also be indexed at $200.
You can judge costs on the basis of the micro-economic studies which can be performed as background for such a plan. In case the House is wondering about relevance, the clause has to do with indexing, and that is what I am talking about. I happened to be here in 1944 when we passed the first Family Allowances Act under which we provided payments of $6, $7 or $8 a month, depending upon the age of the child. A little later on the $7 was raised to $8, so there were only two categories. However, we went more than 25 years before that amount was changed. An amount which meant something when it came into effect in 1945 became meaningless in the late sixties and early seventies. Finally we raised the amount and provided for its indexation. That is a principle to which I think we must adhere without any question.
I point out that we have provided for the indexing of many other things such as old age security, the guaranteed income supplement, veterans pensions under the Pension Act, war veterans allowances, public service pensions, and others. I point out also that my friends in the Progressive Conservative party led a strong campaign over a number of years for the indexing of the exemption levels under the Income Tax Act. The government finally came through with that, and the Progressive Conservatives took credit for it. That does not bother me one way or the other, but the point is that we have it in all these other programs, and not to have full indexing of the family allowance program would be a hoax so far as the mothers and the families of this country are concerned.
I should like to emphasize again that this clause is right. That is why I am prepared to support it wholeheartedly. It is known and accepted that the basic amount of the family allowance is to be indexed starting in 1980. It is to be indexed from the $20 in 1979. However, if that is all that was done, the whole thing would soon get out of kilter. If we were to index the $20 but not the $200 and not the $18,000 cut-off figure, it would be a matter of only a few years before the whole thing would be out of balance. It seems to me that the only way to put this program on a fair and proper basis is to index all three elements. The indexing of the basic amount, which will be $20 in 1979, is provided elsewhere in the legislation, but what is before us now is the proposal to index the $200 tax credit each year and the $18,000 cut-off level. It is my view that these things are right, and that is why we should support them.
I have listened to the discussions about costs, and I will say that 1 think the answers which the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance gave were a bit ingenious when they pointed out that we are saving money because we will not be
Family Allowances
paying that $8 next year and so forth, but I am not bothered by that because I look at this matter from a broad perspective.
I think it is perfectly true-and I see no reason why the government should not admit it-that both the family allowance payments and the tax credits will cost more in actual dollars in 1980 than they will cost in 1979. They will cost more in 1981 than they will cost in 1980, but the thing to bring into this picture is that this indexing is being done in accordance with the consumer price index. It is not being done according to a wage index.
There are times-many workers are experiencing such times right now-when wage increases do not match increases in the cost of living. However, over the long haul, if we look at statistics for a 40, 50 or 60-year period, the tendency is for wages to rise faster than prices and for the total package of income from wages and salaries to keep moving up. The revenue which the federal government gets by way of taxation is geared to the rise in incomes, and this means that when we index all three elements of the family allowance, the basic $20, the $200 tax credit and the $18,000 level, we are indexing those only in accordance with the rise in the consumer price index. However, since the income which the government will get from taxes is related to increases in wages and salaries, the percentage of the total revenue which will be spent on family allowances will decline.
Granted, in absolute dollars the amount paid out will go up. There is no question about that, but I submit that the argument I am making is valid. I argue that as a percentage of the country's total income it will decline, and I say that for there to be any question about this principle being applied to all elements of the family allowance program is a mistake, and I am very pleased to hear the hon. member for St. John's East state that he and his party support the principle which is in clause 2.
The only thing that worried me when I looked at this clause was the explanatory note on the opposite page. It worried me only for a split second, but I think I should indicate the worry I had anyway. The explanatory note says:

The amounts of $200 and $18,000 referred to in subsection 122.2(1)... shall be adjusted annually-
-in accordance with the rise in the consumer price index.

time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills and Standing Orders.
He said: Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to thank hon. members, and particularly the member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), for allowing me to proceed with Bill S-8 at this time. Since this bill was introduced in the other place by Senator Mcllraith and has been studied by the Senate Standing Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs, my remarks will be brief and, I hope, to the point.
The purpose of this bill is to revive the company known as J. H. Poitras & Son Ltd. This company was incorporated in 1965 and had its principal place of business in the city of Hull, Quebec. The company sells, services, and instals fire protection equipment such as fire extinguishers, as well as fire and burglar alarm systems, in the Ottawa-Hull area.
In September, 1977, the present owner of the company decided to sell his shares to another company. In the course of completing the documentation arising from that sale, it was discovered by the lawyer that the company had been dissolved in 1968. The reason was failure to file with the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, for three consecutive years, the annual information returns required under the Canada Corporations Act. It was discovered also that the notices from Consumer and Corporate Affairs requesting the filing of returns did not come to the attention of the company. These notices were sent not to the company's own address but to its lawyer.
The notices were of course published in the Canada Gazette but were apparently not read by the company. In any case, no returns were filed and the company was dissolved before the new owner, Normand St. James, acquired shares in it.
The petitioner, Normand St. James, and the original owner of the company were not aware of the dissolution of the business. Mr. St. James carried on his activities despite the fact that unknown to him no corporate body existed.
In the circumstances, this bill asks that the company be revived and that it be deemed not to have been dissolved. This would regularize the situation. If it is agreeable to the House, 1 would propose that if second reading is granted, the bill be referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills for study.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) has, indeed, consulted with respect to this matter. He was good enough to supply me with copies of minutes from the other place and a record of the debate in the Senate in respect of this bill.
It is really an astounding matter. It is not altogether surprising that a notice might not be referred to the company, but what is surprising to me is this: notwithstanding the fact that the company in question had died in law, and that its death had been duly noted in the records of the government through the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, another department of the government, the Department of National

Revenue, should continue to collect taxes from this corporate corpse. On the other hand, there is no reason why this House, or any member of it, ought not, in the circumstances, to deal appropriately with an agency or a citizen coming to parliament for relief.
I gather from the debate which took place elsewhere that if this House does not deal expeditiously with the matter, as the Senate did, an innocent party would be placed at considerable disadvantage. Thus, on behalf of my hon. friends I am prepared to let this matter go and consent to the reference to the committee as proposed by the hon. member.
I know that in referring to the Canada Gazette as a document which was not read by the proprietor of the company who was so innocently misled, he was not implying that the Canada Gazette was on the best-sellers list by any means-it is a publication which is not always read even by some members of the bar. I appreciate the detail which the hon. member has supplied other members of the House with regard to this matter, and we should certainly like to see the bill dealt with as expeditiously as possible.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REPLACEMENT OF DOMINION DAY BY CANADA DAY
speechtext:
that Bill C-232, to amend the Holidays Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill, which I have introduced in every session of parliament since 1 came here, has been the subject of fairly lively discussion each time it has been brought forward. I must admit that I was somewhat surprised that it was called so early in this session. I note that there are about 25 private bills ahead of this one on the order paper, and I am concerned because 25 members who have put bills on the order paper are not prepared to discuss them at this time. However, that is their business. I am certainly ready to go ahead with any one of my bills, and this one happens to be the first on the list.
Holidays Act
This bill was debated fairly fully in this House on March 14, 1975. At that time it was decided to refer the subject matter of the bill to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
In my opinion, what this bill seeks to do is regularize a situation which for all practical purposes is a fait accompli. In most parts of the country the July 1 holiday is at the present time designated Canada Day. However, according to our statutes it is still Dominion Day. As soon as one talks about changing the name of the holiday from Dominion Day to Canada Day, there are some stalwart supporters of the word "dominion" who immediately rise and exclaim that we are trying to do away with old traditions and so forth.
As someone who was born in Great Britain, who came to this country as an immigrant, and who likes tradition, parades and so forth, I am not overawed by the suggestion that we should be respecting certain old traditions and guarding the word "dominion" in our statutes. Whether we change the name legally now is probably of very little consequence because for all practical purposes, as I have already said, from coast to coast we use the present terminology "Canada Day", and we use it with pride when we refer to the anniversary of the founding of our nation.
There has been some concern about this change among members of the Royal Canadian Legion. I am a member of the Royal Canadian Legion, an ex-serviceman, an ex-military man. I understand the concern of the Royal Canadian Legion.
I understand its feeling about the word "dominion", but I suggest to the Royal Canadian Legion, and to everyone who is concerned about the use of the word "dominion", that in a country with the difficulties we are experiencing today it is a relatively minor matter to eliminate a word, despite all its history and ancient significance. Surely the name of the day which should be of major significance to all of us, July 1, should be acceptable to all Canadians. I say "all Canadians" advisedly, because even those people who speak against this change have not, at least to my knowledge, spoken against the terminology "Canada Day". They speak for retention of "Dominion" without speaking against the word "Canada".
I think there is little else to be said. I honestly believe that this bill is just a tidying up. There are few people left in this country who do not recognize that the connotation which is attached to the word "dominion" is divisive in itself. It is an ancient terminology. It has a significance which is certainly not helpful in uniting all parts of the country today.
In terms of importance perhaps the name "Canada Day" has little significance in that, as I have previously said, it is now a fait accompli. However, in terms of significance to a certain section of the population in this country which does not like the somewhat subservient nature of the word "dominion", it is important. For these reasons I strongly urge passage of Bill C-232, which would change the terminology "Dominion Day" to the popularly acclaimed and generally used "Canada Day".

November 30, 1978
Holidays Act

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REPLACEMENT OF DOMINION DAY BY CANADA DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), I am a little amazed that this bill came up as early on the agenda for the session as it did.
I want to take exception to one expression used by the hon. member twice, and that is that Canada Day is a fait accompli. I am not at all sure it is. To any Canadian, whether of British birth or, as I am, descended from parents of British birth, or who has been here eight or ten generations or who has just come off the boat from Europe or other countries, the word "Canada" has a very special meaning. I do not disagree that the expression "Canada Day" has been used a great deal, whether appropriately or not. However, I think this is important, particularly to the people I represent, many of whom are descendants of United Empire Loyalists.
I do not downgrade the hon. member at all, but I think that a matter of this significance should not be brought up in a private member's bill. The government has been using the expression "Canada Day" for the past few years. If the government wishes to use that name, it should bring in legislation changing the name of the holiday. This is an important matter. I was not here at the time, but we all know about the debates in this House on the flag. Many institutions debated long, hard, and sometimes bitterly about the flag.
The hon. member mentioned one institution, the Royal Canadian Legion, of which he is a member. I am proud to be an honorary member of Branch 99. I think perhaps you, Mr. Speaker, would remember the lengthy flag debate. I know others in the House remember. It was a very acrimonious debate, but because there was an act of parliament all Canadians are now prepared to accept the new flag. A few, of course, would like to have the old one, and I admit that in my heart there is a warm spot for it, but I think most Canadians now accept the new flag.
We have that new flag because of a debate in this House. There was a vote in this House. There was proper committee scrutiny and finally a decision of this House that Canada would have a new flag.
I do not think this matter is a party matter, but if this new name is to be accepted by all Canadians, it should be dealt with in this House as a matter of importance. I think there would be acceptance from many parts of the House and I think there would be considerable debate on the matter, but I do not think it should be taken lightly as a matter to be considered during private members' hour and to be given less than an hour of debate on a quiet Thursday afternoon, with just a few dozen of us in the House who are regularly here at this time of the day. I really do not think this is the time to slip a matter of this importance through the House. I think the matter deserves full debate.
I have to correct the hon. member on the slip that he made when he asked us to pass the bill. If we allowed it, it would be given second reading, approval in principle, and then would go to committee. But it would be wrong to send it to the commit-

tee without the full weight of a debate in parliament and without the weight of government support.
I have said virtually all I want to say on the matter. I will be interested to see, in fact, if members on the government benches are prepared to let this bill go through. If they are, then it would be a very interesting situation.

I believe that this act is a step in the right direction. However, I would point out that the hon. member is correct in assuming that if this bill is passed by us here today, it will go into committee, be debated there, and then will come back to the House and be debated here again. So there will be a great deal of discussion of the matter and, I hope, a great deal of deep thinking about it before the bill is passed and becomes a fait accompli.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about this bill in the context of my riding. The census of 1971 showed that 69 per cent of all the people whom I represent in St. Catharines list their home origin as the British Isles. Notwithstanding that fact and the great tie and great love they have for tradition and for things that are British, the majority of the people in my riding, I believe, would be in favour of calling Dominion Day on July 1, Canada Day.
As you know, this day is currently designated as Dominion Day in the act, but I think most hon. members would agree that over the past few years there has been a growing feeling that such a designation is no longer suitable or desirable. Indeed, throughout what is now almost a decade, it is on what is known to many as Canada Day, Canada Week, and Festival Canada, that millions of Canadians have celebrated the birthday of our nation. I submit that the official designation of July 1 as Canada Day would reflect accurately the feelings of Canadians.
November 30, 1978

The hon. member referred also to the flag debate. I make no apology for taking great pride in the fact that after 98 years we finally chose a flag that is uniquely our own. A great many debates took place across Canada in which people from all walks of life and from all regions had something to say about whether or not we wanted our very own flag. I am an honorary member of the Legion, Branch 24, in St. Catharines. When I went back to my riding on Remembrance Day to join the veterans of the two world wars who marched on that day, it seemed to me as if hundreds of years had passed since we had debated so vehemently whether or not we should have our own flag. As I travel around the world, 1 feel, as do other hon. members and other citizens of Canada, a great deal of pride when I see our very own flag raised.
Let me point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that on November 5 of this year I represented the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) at the ceremony in Vimy marking the sixtieth anniversary of the end of World War I. During my stay in Europe I visited many Commonwealth war graves. These graves, where our soldiers, our fellow Canadians, our brothers and sisters of another year lay buried, had the maple leaf engraved on their headstones, an emblem of Canada which was chosen many years ago, the emblem which we display so proudly on our flag.
I know it may be argued that the designation "Dominion Day" is somehow related to the historical development of Canada and that it should be retained for reasons of tradition, nostalgia, and so on. However, I would like to think that Canada has undergone great and vital growth and has emerged from the colonial status and, in the process, has acquired strength, independence, and a sense of identity, and that therefore Dominion Day is no longer a suitable title for that day set aside for all Canadians, Canadians of all origins and from all regions, to celebrate Canada's birthday and to take pride and joy in being Canadian.

Most of us think of the day as Canada Day, feel it to be Canada Day, refer to it as Canada Day, and celebrate it as Canada Day. 1 say we should therefore call it just that, that is, Canada Day. But I wish to make it clear that I am not belittling the importance of tradition. No, that is the furthest thing from my mind, because our roots run deep to all the great countries and cultures in Europe.
We have emerged with our own Canadian culture, and I think we must recognize that fact over and over again, if needs be, because it took us 111 years to become the Canadians we are today. We did not just happen in the last 12 years, notwithstanding the fact that we have had our very own flag only since 1965. I believe that without a tradition a nation cannot be said to exist. Indeed, 1 do not believe a nation can exist without the traditions and the roots we acknowledge here today.
Holidays Act
I am sensitive to the concerns of those who, in perceiving the importance of tradition, question closely all proposed changes, however seemingly superficial. Without such questioning there would be no balance, there would be nothing to impede those more interested in change for the sake of change. Indeed, it has been due to the efforts of those who are convinced that tradition has an important role to play in the forging of national identity that much of our heritage has been preserved, many of our traditions retained.

I cannot lend support to any move which I consider to be detrimental to any part of the fabric of Canadian heritage. I do not endorse change for its own sake. great country of Canada. Mr. Speaker, I support such initiatives. The fact of wanting to confirm the designation of Canada Day for July 1 instead of the name Dominion Day seems to me an initiative which aims precisely at strengthening our sense of belonging to Canada in the present context of Canadian unity problems.
In my opinion, the fact of being able once a year on July 1 to celebrate the day of a country called Canada reminds me of the importance of living in total harmony and also in strict equality among the two great founding peoples of this country, that is the French and the English. We have a very vast country where many cultures co-exist in what is commonly called multiculturalism, but two great peoples have contributed to build a society inspired on the one hand by French humanism and on the other hand by British parliamentarian-ism. This is a very rich heritage that we have been given by two great founding peoples whose languages are French and English, and in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the fact of celebrating each year a national holiday which would be called Canada Day could make us more aware of the wealth of this great country, not only on a material level, but in terms of its origins and of that need to consider the great importance once again of living not only in mutual respect for each other, Mr. Speaker, but also of living together in the strictest equality. And that is what justifies our role as members of parliament from Quebec here in Ottawa in trying to make this country a truly united country in that context. And when we have before us such a legislation to change the name of Dominion Day for Canada Day, we feel more at home, we feel more pride in being Canadians, we feel more authenticity, and we feel better prepared to live in harmony and on equal terms in this land of ours.
Mr. Speaker, I think we must not overdo traditions. There is a right balance to keep, and I always have had much respect for the saying In medio stat virtus, virtue stands between extremes, and I feel that traditions in certain instances, 1 imagine, have to be respected, but one has also to be realistic and try to present and support measures which make us live according to the reality. Yesterday is gone, Mr. Speaker, tomorrow is yet to come, the present is today. I suggest that we should forget the past somewhat more easily to avoid nostalgia, that we should not live too much in the future to avoid anxiety and that we should be practical and live in the present and in the reality.
And today, Mr. Speaker, when we just had federal-provincial conferences, whether on the constitution or the economy, and that we realize a tendency to hoard a bigger share of the pie, to monopolize, to be selfish, we realize, I think, the importance of having a Canadian government, a federal government, a central government really representative of our two great funding nations and strong enough to maintain unity at the constitutional level and to make sure that our two great linguistic communities will live together with equal opportuni-

Mr. Chairman, yesterday I was talking about the effect this bill would have upon the status Indians. I am sure this question comes under clause 2 which we are presently discussing and that this is a suitable point at which to make my comments.
The Indian people of Canada have been given little time to review the implications of Bill C-10, not having been invited to comment on it until the meeting between the minister and the National Indian Brotherhood on November 14, 1978. In spite of the brief time for consultation among Indian people, there are a number of concerns about the bill that they would like to raise, as well as to offer two amendments to the bill that would help resolve these difficulties.
For many reasons, Indians in Canada historically and traditionally have not been and should not be part of the process of

November 30, 1978
Family Allowances
taxation of income. Freedom from taxation is one of the fundamental rights the original occupants of this land possessed, this being but a partial compensation for the land originally occupied by them. This relationship was and still is an understood condition of the treaties, and of the establishment of the reserve system. Parliament recognized tax exemption of Indians in the Indian Act itself.
In spite of these previous understandings, the Indian exemption status has been subjected to what appears to be a planned, progressive erosion by government forces. The government, through its Ministry of National Revenue and that ministry's departmental bureaucrats, has been using tax questions as a form of unjustified harassment of Indian people, both at the Indian organizational level and the individual level. This harassment is on the increase, and the department is expanding its attempts to collect income tax from Indians engaged in their traditional pursuits, especially trapping.
The Indian people of Canada have no choice, therefore, but to view Bill C-10 as yet another surreptitious attempt by government to establish a mechanism for taxation of Indian people on Indian lands, this time by arbitrarily indexing all Indian mothers into the tax system through mandatory acquisition of social insurance numbers and the filing of income tax returns prior to receiving the child tax credit.
Is it fair and just to ask the mothers of the most impoverished and disadvantaged group of this country to forgo the very much needed financial benefits offered by this bill in order to protect the Indian people from the bill's inbuilt potential for violation of their traditional and historical rights?
The National Indian Brotherhood has another great concern. The requirements for receiving the tax credit-those of acquiring a social insurance number and fding an income tax return-would prove quite complicated to many thousands of Indian mothers who have relatively negligible experience in matters of business and paperwork when compared to their non-Indian counterparts. I mentioned this in my remarks yesterday, Mr. Chairman. There is a strong likelihood that as a result of this requirement a significant number of Indian mothers will not receive the tax credit to which they are entitled.
Reports from departmental officials indicate that between 15 per cent to 25 per cent of pensioners eligible for the guaranteed income supplement do not receive it. We expect that the percentage of Indian mothers not receiving the child tax credit will be at least as high. Suppose that 20 per cent of the qualified mothers were not receiving child tax credit because the forms had not been completed or because they did not understand how to obtain it. A large sum is involved here. Twenty per cent of the $14 million which, we are told, would go to the status Indian mothers on reserves amounts to about $2.8 million.
The government has offered a small amount of assistance to Indian mothers as far as the paperwork is concerned, but the National Indian Brotherhood strongly feels that this will not be adequate to ensure that the tax credit will be distributed as planned.

A further concern is that the payment of the credit in one lump sum annually will likely lead to unwise spending of the money by families unused to handling such large amounts at one time. We discussed this yesterday. I brought up this question of the lump sum payment to Indian mothers and pointed out the difficulty they would experience in cashing these cheques. Further, it might not be easy for the mothers concerned to understand that, because of the $8 increase in family allowance per child and the nature of the lump sum payment, they would have to distribute it over a seven or eight month period. If this is not well understood, perhaps the money will be spent unwisely. I am glad to have this opinion confirmed by the National Indian Brotherhood. Unwise use of this money by people unused to receiving money in lump sums could have harmful consequences, including even family breakdown.
The National Indian Brotherhood suggests that the department should be considering putting out a special form distinct from the income tax return form and devised especially for use by status Indian mothers. They suggest that this form be considered complete with the use of the mother's band number, and that a social insurance number should not be required. It is well known that all status Indians have a number. They keep this number from birth until death and they refer to it frequently. I cannot understand why Indian mothers should be required to have a social insurance number in order to qualify for the child tax credit. Status Indians living on reserves do not have to pay income tax. I ask the minister to pay particular attention to this request.
The second suggestion the National Indian Brotherhood made is that the child tax credit be paid in quarterly instalments rather than in a single annual payment at the option of the mother.

It is a new principle as far as the Income Tax Act is concerned. The principle of family income has not been written into the Income Tax Act before. It is the first time a provision is being put into the Income Tax Act based on the joint income of spouses.
The minister refuses to acknowledge any connection between the joint income provision in this bill and the principle of joint filing. She has discounted it on a number of occasions. Whether there is a single sheet of paper on which both incomes are added together or whether there is a joint, complex tax form is quite beside the point. It is important to point out that the filing unit for the purpose of the child tax credit is the husband and wife, if both are working. This is very clearly stated in this clause.
I refer the minister to a document that was put out by the Minister of Finance on November 16, the night of the budget. This is a document which dealt with filing units. The document is called "Integration of Social Program Payments into the Income Tax System". In this booklet the Minister of Finance deals with four options of filing units for the purposes

of the income-tested refundable tax credits. The four options include (1) the individual; (2) the primary earner-this is the spouse with the higher income; (3) the primary earner plus spouse; and (4) the family, including children. This clause that the minister has before us clearly uses the third option that the Minister of Finance presented in his integration of social program payments into the income tax system. In this document the minister speaks about this particular option; that is, the primary earner plus spouse; the husband plus the secondary earner, which is the wife. At page 14 of this document he says;
However, a move to any type of "joint filing" for purposes of the Income Tax Act would be very significant, both conceptually and in terms of administrative complexity.
The Minister of Finance recognizes that there is a connection between the two. He considers it very significant. At page 19 of this document, under the heading "Family-Based Benefit and Income-Testing", the statement appears:
Since supplementation is intended to assist low-income families, it would be appropriate to adopt a fding unit which included both spouses.... As noted under general features, any move to "joint" or "family" filing for purposes of calculating a tax credit would involve major changes to the present tax system.
That is the point I want to underline, that the Minister of Finance said it would involve major changes to the present tax system. However, the Minister of National Health and Welfare when she was responding to me earlier in this debate passed it off as having very little meaning whatsoever. I was glad to read that the Minister of Finance recognized that the introduction of the concept of family income into the Income Tax Act is a very major step. On the other hand, the Minister of National Health and Welfare denies there is anything new in the family income provision. It is just the same old thing, she said; all the other programs are based on it.
This is the first time it is built into the income tax provisions. That is what is new. That is what is different, and that is what is major about it. I ask the minister, does she disagree with the Minister of Finance on the significance of this step that is being taken in introducing the family income provision into the Income Tax Act? Does she agree with him that it is a major step or doesn't she? The other night she dismissed it and said that it was already in practice. I would like to ask her as well if she disagrees-and I quote the Minister of Finance-if this step comes under any move to joint or family filing for purposes of calculating a tax credit. The other night the minister dismissed that as well. I hope that she will not answer as she did the other night, when she said that the income tax form used is "just a slip of paper".
I have attempted previously to express to the minister my concern about the concept of family income based, as it is in this bill, on marital status. I have expressed my concern that it is a regressive step to put such a principle in the Income Tax Act at a time when the human rights commissioner is looking into all legislation, but especially if he is looking into the Income Tax Act for discriminatory clauses. This is also a time when society is in transition, a time when a more complex analysis of household units and income would make much better sense.
November 30, 1978

I have raised this matter, as the minister knows, on several occasions. The family income provision in this bill is discriminatory since it is based on the marital status of the individuals concerned. I have read the particular portion of this clause which sets this out clearly. The commissioner of human rights has written to the Minister of Finance expressing his concern about assessing family income as a basis for taxation and social policy. Perhaps the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance could tell me whether the Minister of Finance has responded to the concern shown by the human rights commissioner. The commissioner wrote:
We would like to be assured that the government does not intend to base its future taxation and social policies on the joint income of two spouses, which is not an adequate definition of family income.
That is the definition we find in the bill. The commissioner goes on to state in his letter of November 2, 1978:
The basic principle of using the income of the total family or living group will require extensive examination before its implications are fully appreciated.
I should like to know what views the Minister of Finance expressed in response to his letter.
Aside from the fact that the family income provision discriminates against couples who are married, the principle falls back on the notion of dependency against which women have been fighting for many years. I would have expected the minister to have recognized this. The assumption inherent in the bill is that a man who earns $5,000 or $20,000 or $50,000 shares that income equitably with his family. We all know that in law a wife has no claim on her husband's salary. She may be entitled to half the house should the marriage dissolve, but she is not entitled to half the monthly pay cheque as long as the marriage holds together. The family income provision in this bill presumes that married people pool their income and share it. I hope that is true in many cases but I am sure that in many other cases it is not. Large numbers of married women go out to work to improve their economic status and that of their children. They may need an individual income because they do not get a fair share of the husband's income.
That is the reality of the world we live in, yet this clause proposes to lock into legislation a presumption that the husband automatically shares his income with the wife. The wife becomes a dependant who is looked after by the husband at all times. The family income provision lumps the income of the wife with that of the husband and assumes it to be one income. As a result, many thousands of married working women will be deprived of the child tax credit. As long as women on the whole make significantly less money than men, and as long as they have no claim in law to their husband's income, the family income provision as set out in this clause will hurt them. As long as married working women are looked upon as an excuse for high unemployment figures, as long as their income is regarded as secondary income, any kind of family income provisions will work against their attempt at equality in the work force and in the home.
I should also like to ask the minister what kind of study went into the family income provision as set out in this clause.

This amounts to economic independence in the hands of women. It is exactly what I wanted, and I am very pleased about it. It is money for children, but it must go through the hands of adults. Of course, she will declare, whenever it applies, all moneys or other payments she receives on behalf of her children because those are forms of family income.
This is no discrimination. If there was need for proof, and that is the ultimate proof-I regret it in a sense because it means an additional paper burden on women in the country- each partner in a family will have to file an income tax form separately. So individual taxation, which is the key to the taxation system in Canada, is totally respected here. I hope that next year we will be able to have only one form for the 1.5 million mothers who do not file an income tax return. 1 cannot repeat more clearly that this bill reflects the reality that children depend on parental resources and that parents are jointly responsible for their children. Nothing is more basic to our society or to any society, and that is what the women's movement has strived for.
I could speak and speak on this subject because it is one of my favourite topics. It happens that I want to do things that will help women take their full place in society and get what they are entitled to. Today I am sponsoring a bill which discriminates in their favour, and I am proud of it. I ask: Is the hon. member opposed to the GIS procedure by which every month both partners in a marriage put their income together and declare it so as to get the supplement? What is wrong with that?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHILD TAX CREDIT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHILD TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the short time remaining I want simply to point out to the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands that no party has a monopoly on fighting discrimination. Certainly if you look at the statements I have made-I admit I am not the kind of member to whom one would instantly refer while reading Hansard-you would find that on November 7 I raised this matter with the minister and with her colleague. We were sitting in almost the same places and we discussed precisely this isssue which was raised at that time by Mr. Fairweather of the human rights commission. So I do not think she can say that this party has been either silent or unconcerned about whether or not there are discriminatory elements in this aspect of the bill.
However, I think the issue is a little more complex than the hon. member has allowed, for the very simple reason that what we are trying to do in this bill, as I understand it-we support it, I want to make that perfectly clear, but I am certainly not sure where the hon. member for York-Simcoe stands on the
Family Allowances
bill after having heard him this evening-is not simply to deal with whether a woman or a husband can file separately. That is not the only issue.
The other question is, what is the income of the household unit, of the family unit which is supporting a child or children. It is a middle class illusion of the worst kind to think that we cannot take into account the income of the family unit because it would give rise to all kinds of other discrimination of an economic nature that is much more profound.
What will you do in a situation where a middle-class lawyer or doctor is earning $40,000, $50,000 or $60,000 a year, his wife is not working because she has children and they have decided that that is the way they want to do things, so she is not making any money? That is a household unit supporting a family. It would be highly inequitable if the poorer members of this population were to support the children of that family because we were allowed to carry out a bourgeois illusion-if I may use that word in the House-that the woman was independent in that situation.
In this situation we are looking at the whole family unit, and we have to ask ourselves not only whether there is discrimination against women, but whether there is discrimination of an economic kind and the money is getting to the people who really need it. That seems to be the critical question.
I have some concerns, which I have already expressed to the minister and to the parliamentary secretary, in that I am not sure that the wording in section 121.1(a) as it now stands really addresses itself to the reality. The reality is that a family unit today is much more broadly defined. Here I agree with the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, who brought out the same point. Today, the family unit is much more complex than this bill allows for.
I do not wish to put forward an amendment tonight, so I will give the minister notice of the amendment which I propose to bring forward on Tuesday. It will take into account the fact that we have to deal with common law relationships where people are not necessarily married but nevertheless are providing a joint income for the support of the child, and it will deal with a form which will be quite separate from the income tax form, as the minister has already said-and I was delighted to hear it. There is no reason why we cannot have the concept of a family income or household income, and a definition of a household which will ensure that there are no inequities in this system. I gave an example on November 7 but I will give it again. If you have two common law spouses living together and, let us say, they have been separated from their previous marriages, and they have children from those marriages to support but they do not happen to be married, and both happen to have a sizeable income, it would be discriminatory to give that upper middle-class family with a high standard of living a benefit to which they are not entitled in economic or social terms.
I want to say on behalf of my party that the real discrimination with which we are concerned-we have expressed our concern for women, youth and the unemployment problem yesterday and today in committee and in the House and we

November 30, 1978
Adjournment Debate
will continue to do that-is the fact that we want to be certain that under the bill the money will go to those households and families where there is a need for it; and we want to ensure that we keep intact the redistributive effects of this bill. We congratulate the government on the redistributive intent in the bill and we want to see it preserved.
