ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-FIREARMS CONTROL PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 14 a Montreal newpaper, The Gazette, published in its daily edition a disturbing article, under the circumstances, about the restricted firearms recall campaign undertaken by the Canadian government. With your leave, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote a few excerpts of that article entitled:
Guns amnesty may misfire, police fear.
Operation Exchange-the two week old amnesty campaign started by the federal government to encourage people to hand over illegal or restricted firearms-appears headed for failure in Quebec.
Police believe there are about 10,000 illegal firearms in Quebec but say this year's program will fail unless the government steps up its publicity campaign.
"Many people aren't aware of the amnesty program because of poor publicity," said Quebec Police Force Constable Marcel Belanger.

Such are the comments of Mr. Steven Kowch, if my pronunciation is correct, which led me on the following day to direct to the Solicitor General a question which appears on page 1149 of Hansard and which was stated as follows:
With regard to the restricted firearms recall campaign undertaken by the Canadian government and more particularly by his department, could the minister tell the House and the Canadian public whether it is true that this campaign has had disappointing results in the province of Quebec? At the same time, could he indicate whether this campaign is having encouraging results in other parts of Canada?
[Mr. Rae.J
If, in his answer, the Solicitor General said he was satisfied and very much encouraged by the results of that campaign among the general public, he was far from answering my concern about the results of that operation in Quebec, which arose from the statements made by Mr. Kowch. If encouraging, an accurate answer would have enabled me to ignore the statements published in the Gazette, and consequently to regard them as a reinstatement of the frequent regard and absolutely political criticism of the relations between the Government of Canada and the province of Quebec. The people of my province want only to feel as completely secure as possible, and consequently they would have also welcomed a clear answer with some relief. As a result of this incomplete reply by the minister, the concern which Steven Kowch's remarks had raised in me, instead of being dispelled or reduced, increased.
You are certainly aware, Mr. Speaker, that this campaign- which by the way is supposed to end today, unless it was extended-is part of a process initiated by the Solicitor General of Canada to encourage Canadians to register their restricted weapons or get rid of them if they want to. The public must also understand that this service was set up to protect individuals from a possible accusation of simple possession of illegal weapons as provided under the act. Hon. members, needless to say, need not being reminded that the government, in order to maintain law and order in this era of violence which began several years ago, had come to the conclusion that it was necessary to reinforce the Canadian statutes dealing with gun control and introduced a legislation which was adopted by parliament in 1977 and entered into force on January 1, 1978.
We should consider that over a five year period before the adoption of this gun control act, the number of casualties due to firearms increased constantly every year. For instance, the number of suicides which account for the greater part of these casualties increased by 17.12 per cent, the numbers of murders or homicides increased by 27.10 per cent, while, accidents decreased by 19.82 per cent. There is no longer any need to prove the relevance of this measure passed in 1977. That is why, Mr. Speaker, the article I referred to at the beginning of my remarks has created some concern in my mind and among a large sector of the people in Quebec. In the hope of obtaining tonight a clear and precise answer, I will again put this question to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General: With regard to the restricted firearms recall campaign undertaken by the Canadian government and more particularly by his department, could he tell the House and the Canadian public whether it is true that this campaign has had disappointing results in the province of Quebec? At the same time, could he tell us whether this campaign is having more encouraging results in other parts of Canada?

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Young (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-FIREARMS CONTROL PROGRAM-REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member last queried the
November 30, 1978

Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) on the results of the firearms amnesty program in Quebec and other regions of Canada, the program was only at its halfway mark and results were available only for the first ten days. It was, therefore, difficult at that point to make an accurate forecast of the final outcome.
Today at midnight the program comes to an end. Figures released today by the Solicitor General make it clear that the program has in fact been a resounding success. With statistics only up to November 24, the national total stands at 23,331; that is, firearms of all types brought forward for registration or disposal. I am confident that by the time the results of the last six days are tallied we will be very comfortably over the 30,000 mark for the entire month. That is 1,000 guns a day, most of them illegally held guns now made legal, but large numbers also being unwanted guns turned in in the interest of safety. This demonstrates a tremendous vote of confidence in the gun control program on the part of the public.
I also wish to stress that, based on figures available to date, the program has been a success in all parts of Canada, including Quebec, where for years the authorities have been actively encouraging owners of illegal weapons to bring them forward to police for legalization or disposal.
It has been said that the Quebec figures were too low. Indeed, if one judges only by the rough statistics, of the more than 23,000 guns received to date, Quebec was responsible for only 1,300 or so, while Ontario accounted for over 10,000, over 80 per cent of the guns in all cases being handguns.
In fact, those figures should be analysed in relation to the gun ownership pattern across the country. Quebec, for instance, holds only 8.1 per cent of all the handguns in Canada, according to an extensive gun survey done in 1976 by Statistics Canada. Under amnesty, they account for 5.2 per cent of all handguns brought in across Canada. Although this is slightly below their share of the national stock, the discrepancy is probably more than offset by the fact that under its unofficial amnesty policy, Quebec received about 2,500 such weapons in 1977 alone. It is fair to say that most of those guns would otherwise have quite probably turned up this year. This parallel holds true for other regions, none of which is very far above or below its share of the national stock.
Our Quebec figures are a little bit light due to difficulties in obtaining returns from certain districts. Full figures for all regions will be available next week and I am sure they will confirm that the program has been totally successful in all parts of the country.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD-PURCHASE OF HOPPER CARS BY BOARD-CONSULTATION WITH RAILWAYS
CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD-PURCHASE OF HOPPER CARS BY BOARD-CONSULTATION WITH RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am taking part in the debate tonight because of a three-part question I put on November 28 to the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board. My question was inspired by an announcement that the Canadian Wheat Board was tendering for 2,000 hopper cars to be purchased out of the
Adjournment Debate
proceeds of the sale of producers' grain, and the government was using as its authority section 4(4)(d) of the Canadian Wheat Board Act which gives the board the power:
-to acquire, hold and dispose of real and personal property, but the board shall not acquire or dispose of any real property without the approval of the governor in council;
The first part of my question asked if there was a need for these cars. The minister presently has a study costing $650,000 under way on this very subject. The second part of the question asked if producer groups had been consulted. Despite what the minister says, Mr. Speaker, no farm groups were consulted. The advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board, however, was consulted, but this group ceases its functions very soon when their terms expire, and a new committee is about to be elected.
The third part of my question asked if any new or innovative ideas were forthcoming to improve the situation at Vancouver, to which the minister replied no, there were no new ideas.
We see this move as a breach of the spirit of the National Transportation Act. In effect, what it does is change the statutory freight rates on grain without consulting parliament. It is unprecedented in the 40 years of Canadian Wheat Board operations. On this side of the House we feel that the Canadian Wheat Board has been an outstanding example of the implementation of government in action on behalf of the individual producers. It must be assisted by the national government, and we want to keep it that way.
I fear, because the present minister has let things slide so badly, that the board probably had no alternative but to take this unprecedented action in order to focus national attention on transportation problems. This government has a responsibility to act and to act now. The situation at present is that we have greater markets overseas than the Canadian Wheat Board can serve, and there is greater productive capacity on the prairies than our producers have used. The tragedy is that unless this changes there will be no incentive to use the modern technology that is available. It is easier to sell grain now than to transport it to tidewater.
Lost sales, deferred sales, interest and demurrage claims will total well over $500 million this year, something over $4,000 for every permit holder in western Canada. We are sold out right through 1979 and will not be in the market in a meaningful way until after that time. So the story is, lost sales, deferred sales, boats waiting and customers waiting out there.
The question is, how can we make better and more effective use of the system we have? This fall the railways claim that they have unused capacity. If, as they contend they have unused rail capacity in the summer when weather is good, then surely we should be looking at stockpiling or positioning our grain in overseas terminals during that period. It seems to me that in a great port such as Rotterdam there should be a terminal elevator with "Canada" written on it, and a Canadian inspector stationed there so that when a miller sends his barge down the Rhine he will be assured he will be getting the proper

November 30, 1978
Adjournment Debate
grade. We have never allowed one bushel of Canadian wheat to leave this country unsold. I know the old argument, that if you put us in a long position it will force the price down, but in 1978 I cannot buy that.
We have unused capacity at Pacific seaboard in the form of the bulk handling terminals, Canadian Pacific at Port Moodie, Neptune Terminals and Vancouver wharves. These could be used to supplement the existing terminal system at no additional cost. Put the wheat through the terminals, but let us put our feed barley through the bulk handling facilities. Certainly farm run feed barley is equally as good as our export grade. It seems to me that the fastest way to get the price of this grain up is to get rid of it; but instead we continually advertise to the world that we have a tremendous carryover here in Canada of half a billion bushels. Nothing could be more depressing to the world price than a statement like that.
We could have given special over quota privileges at the interior government elevators which would have helped shorten the turnaround time required for the railways. This method was tried in Lethbridge and was found to be very successful. All we needed in Prince Rupert was a commitment by the Canadian Wheat Board and this government that grain would move through there. If this commitment had been given the grain companies themselves would have had terminal facilities at Prince Rupert years ago.
Our western grain farmers go about the business each year of producing wealth for this nation, and I believe that they deserve a better shake than this. It is time for new and innovative ideas as we get ready to move into the 1980s.

speakeroldname: Mr. Hal Herbert (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD-PURCHASE OF HOPPER CARS BY BOARD-CONSULTATION WITH RAILWAYS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question relating to the number of cars we might need is a complex one because we have to know how many times they are turned around between the prairies and Thunder Bay or the west coast. We also have to know if we have a minimum number of cars to meet the needs in ordinary times or peak periods, when necessary, even though it be for only five or six weeks.
Railway companies have argued that the number of cars required would be available but it is still difficult to determine how many cars are required. The Canadian Wheat Board and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), as he stated this afternoon, are convinced we will need more cars in the very near future.
The Canadian Wheat Board may have a different view from the railways as to what constitutes an adequate number of cars. The board must be concerned with the fact that it might have to pay demurrage charges. Consequently the cars that the Board is planning to buy might enable it to avoid demurrage charges in the future during peak periods of market demand.
Producers have the same concerns as the board and when they were consulted they accepted in principle the proposed purchase. These past few days, the minister supported the

steps taken by the Canadian Wheat Board. However, I must also emphasize the other steps taken by the minister. The branch line upgrading program being over, greater and more efficient use will be made of the cars now available and all those the board might acquire later on. In order to ensure better use of the whole system, the minister announced this afternoon the appointment of an analyst to study grain handling and transportation operations and make suggestions for improvements.
The recently released Snavely report indicates that major improvements have already been made with respect to the use of cars. Nevertheless we have to determine whether it is possible to do more and make further improvements as soon as possible. In concluding, I will say that we can prove that the government took a benevolent attitude towards the handling and transportation problems this country is facing.

subtopic: URBAN AFFAIRS-ALLEGED FAILURE OF DEPARTMENT TO PROMOTE HOME INSULATION PROGRAM
URBAN AFFAIRS-ALLEGED FAILURE OF DEPARTMENT TO PROMOTE HOME INSULATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 23 I addressed questions to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) regarding cutbacks amounting to $116 million in the Canadian home insulation program. At that time 1 did not receive satisfactory or substantive answers from either minister.
When the program was unveiled last year it was described by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources as the "key item" in a campaign to reduce the rate of growth of energy use to zero per cent per person by 1985. I do not think anyone would dispute the aims of this program particularly at a time when the conservation of our non-renewable resources is recognized as being more important than ever before. The minister envisioned that CHIP would save this country 50 million barrels of oil a year, which would amount to a saving of $1 billion on the annual cost of imported oil. What is more, the average Canadian who took full advantage of the insulation program could expect to cut his heating bill by 37 per cent. According to the minister, that would amount to a saving of $140 a year for the average family.
After such ambitious beginnings, it was difficult to believe the government announcement that CHIP, barely a year old, would become a victim of this government's misguided restraint program. But it did. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has announced that the CHIP budget has been cut in half, leaving only $116 million to continue the program over the next two years. When I asked the minister if the cutbacks mean the government is abandoning its commitment
November 30, 1978

to help home owners reduce their energy consumption, he replied that it was not. In fact, he suggested he was satisfied with the success of the program and said it would go forward on a much less ambitious scale in future.
Mr. Speaker, I maintain the government is indeed abandoning its energy saving conservation objectives. With funds for the "key item" in its energy conservation program cut in half to $56 million this year and $60 million next year, that conclusion is obvious. These cutbacks in home insulation grants are going to mean a long, cold winter for thousands of homeowners who will be disqualified from the program.
Under CHIP, owners of homes built before 1946 can apply for a grant of up to $350 to cover the cost of insulation materials. As it was originally conceived, the program was to be advanced so that by 1984 all homes built before 1977 would be eligible for grants. The cutbacks mean that the qualifying date for CHIP grants will be held at 1946. This completely disregards the fact that by far the majority of Canadian homes were built after the second world war. Because of the restrictions imposed by the cutbacks, only 20 per cent of Canadian home owners will be able to participate in what is-or was-a very important and beneficial program.
I addressed my supplementary question to the minister of urban affairs, who was responsible for the administration of the Canadian home insulation program through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I regret his answer was no more informative than that supplied by his colleague.
It is a sad fact that only 50,000 of the 1.2 million owners of single unit dwellings eligible for insulation grants have taken advantage of CHIP. I suggested to the minister that the reason for this poor showing was his own department's failure to promote the aims and objectives of the program. The minister preferred to turn this around and he blamed the public for being slow to respond.
The minister's department optimistically claims that more than 100,000 home owners will take advantage of the program next year, which will fulfil all the demand there is. I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that if this program was better promoted, and if eligibility was not limited by budget cutbacks to less than 20 per cent of the home owners in Canada, demand for this program would be increased tenfold.
Energy conservation is no less important today than it was a year ago when CHIP was first introduced. In the process of reducing energy consumption, this program has created jobs and boosted industry. This is not the time to cut back. It will also cut out the creation of jobs in the Canada Works phase 2 for senior citizens and those eligible under the CHIP program. That is another problem that we will have to face this winter. It will add to unemployment.
All in all I was not satisfied with the answer to my questions. I hope the parliamentary secretary will have some good news in his brief remarks.
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. Hal Herbert (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: URBAN AFFAIRS-ALLEGED FAILURE OF DEPARTMENT TO PROMOTE HOME INSULATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this subject was discussed in committee just this afternoon. It is not a question of budget cuts but of utilization of the funds that have been made available. It is true the requests that have been coming have not been coming fast enough to use up the available funds.
When the Canadian Home Insulation Program was first introduced there was concern over the possible impact of such an incentive on the supply and price of insulation materials. As a construction man I was concerned because at that time there was a shortage of insulation materials in the province of Quebec. Even when the program was introduced in Prince Edward Island and another maritime province I was concerned that this would create a further shortage of insulation materials. There was a belief that the manufacturing capacity had not yet been put in place to meet the extra demand that would be stimulated. This was true.
During the preceding summer, manufacturers had not been utilizing their full manufacturing capacity. There was a fear that consumer protection mechanisms had not been sufficiently developed. The government wanted to provide an incentive for people to insulate their homes but it did not want to do so in a way that would result in dislocation of the new housing industry, or put inflationary pressures on materials and cause problems of faulty insulation. Obviously if there had been a bigger demand for insulation materials, it would have had some effect on new house construction.
The nature and amount of grant offered needed to be tailored to a deliberate and responsible introduction of this new factor into the market. Now we have more than a year's experience and it is clear that if the Canadian Home Insulation Program is to meet its targets, some additional inducements will be needed. Obviously the first effort must be to have the older houses well insulated. These are the houses which have the poorest insulation as a general rule. The program has been structured so that these changes can be brought in with a minimum of complication. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation staff have been studying through sample surveys and other means what advice to give to the minister on this matter. He should be in a position to make an announcement within a few weeks.
The home insulation program staff have worked hard and conscientiously to promote the program. Over 272,000 Canadians have been sent application kits, and requests are coming in at the rate of more than 1,500 each week. I have no doubt that ultimately the program can and will achieve its objectives.
In conclusion, I was personally concerned that the demand would be such that the construction market for insulation

products would be disrupted by the program. I expressed that concern to the minister at the time, and I was not then occupying my present position. I feel that the way the program has been introduced is the best way to proceed, and as time progresses I have no doubt whatever that the moneys allowed for this program will be utilized to the full.
